about.text: A thick, curdled, sour fermented milk of southern Africa (also emasi, maas, mafi), eaten in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Lesotho and often compared to cottage cheese or plain yoghurt with a much stronger flavour. Traditionally unpasteurised cow's milk sours in a smoked calabash or skin bag; the watery whey (umlaza) is poured off and the thick curd is amasi.

how.text: Traditional amasi sours on the milk's own flora, in a smoked calabash or skin bag, for one to five days; lactococci dominate, with Leuconostoc and lactobacilli. Commercial amasi (per the Wikipedia article, secondary figures) adds skim milk powder and gelatine, pasteurises, and sets with a Lactococcus lactis starter. The species list is from a background statement in Todorov 2008 citing a South African traditional-fermented-milk reference.

steps.note: The watery whey (umlaza) that separates is poured off.

processing.text: Traditional amasi sours raw cow milk on its own flora over 1-5 d. Commercial amasi is pasteurised (72 °C, 15 s), cooled to 30 °C and set with a Lactococcus lactis starter (about 10^6 cfu/ml) for 16-24 h at 30 °C.
